# Handover

> Handover prepares owner-run businesses in the United States for sale. For a fixed fee it recasts three years of financials to show true owner earnings, analyzes customers and revenue, writes the business's story for buyers, organizes a document room, and gives the owner a fix-it list and an indicative value range. Handover is not a business broker: it does not list businesses, speak to buyers, negotiate or take success fees.

- Who it is for: owners of businesses worth up to about $10 million, typically planning to sell or retire within a few years, and business brokers with sellers who are not yet ready to list.
- Price: free online readiness score and free 45-minute review. Sale-Ready Package from $5,000 (business worth under $1M), $10,000 ($1M–$3M) or $15,000 ($3M–$10M). Fixed fee, no percentage of the sale.
- Timing: a four-week program (kick-off, then documents, numbers, story and hand-back, one week each), about five hours of the owner's time.
- Confidentiality: Handover deals only with the owner and never contacts staff, customers or suppliers.
- Contact: contact@handoveradvisors.com

## Guides
- [How to sell a small business: the steps, in order](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/how-to-sell-a-small-business): Selling a small business takes nine steps: decide what you need, get records a buyer can verify, fix what a buyer would mark down, learn what it is worth, choose how to sell, find buyers, agree the deal, get through due diligence, and close. In the second quarter of 2026, brokers reported averages of six to ten months from engagement to close for businesses valued up to $2 million.
- [Exit planning for a small business: what it is and when to start](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/exit-planning-for-small-business-owners): Exit planning means deciding when you want to leave your business, who will take it over and what you need from the deal, then getting the business ready for that day. Succession planning is the "who takes over" part. Brokers report that most sellers did less than a year of exit planning; our rule of thumb is to start three years or more before you want to be out.
- [Checklist for selling a business: how to prepare it for sale](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/how-to-prepare-a-business-for-sale): Preparing a business for sale means getting five things in order before a buyer looks: financial records a buyer can verify, a business that runs without you, customer numbers that show how concentrated your sales are, paperwork that transfers cleanly, and a price with evidence behind it. The paperwork takes weeks to months. Making the business less dependent on you can take a year or more, so start early.
- [How long does it take to sell a small business?](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/how-long-does-it-take-to-sell-a-small-business): Sales of smaller businesses, those worth under $2 million, averaged six to ten months from engaging a broker to closing in the second quarter of 2026, according to the International Business Brokers Association (IBBA) and M&A Source. Businesses worth $2 million to $50 million averaged 11 to 12 months. Preparing the business beforehand, and any transition period afterwards, add to that.
- [Why won't my business sell? The usual reasons, and what to fix first](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/why-businesses-dont-sell): In the Q4 2022 survey by the International Business Brokers Association and M&A Source, brokers named a price higher than buyers will pay more often than any other reason, in every deal-size band. Some causes are outside your control. Five are yours to work on: your records, your role, your paperwork, your customers and your price. Start with the records.
- [Selling a business by owner or with a broker: fees, pros and cons](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/sell-a-business-by-owner-or-with-a-broker): You can sell a business without a broker, and it is most practical when you already have a likely buyer, such as an employee, a competitor or a customer. A broker is usually paid a success fee at closing, commonly quoted at around 10% of the price on smaller deals, to find and screen buyers and run the process. The records a buyer's lender checks are the same either way.
- [What is seller's discretionary earnings (SDE)? How to calculate it](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/what-is-sellers-discretionary-earnings): Seller's discretionary earnings (SDE) is the total cash flow a business produces for one full-time owner in a year: their pay, perks and profit together. You calculate it by starting with pre-tax profit and adding back the owner's pay, interest, depreciation, amortization, and personal or one-off costs. Brokers report businesses selling for up to $2 million as a multiple of SDE (the price divided by SDE).
- [SDE vs EBITDA: which one will a buyer use to price your business?](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/sde-vs-ebitda): A buyer who will run the business personally usually prices it on seller's discretionary earnings (SDE), which counts all of the owner's pay as profit. A buyer who will hire someone to run it usually uses EBITDA, which charges a market wage for that job first. EBITDA is the smaller number, so the same price is a higher multiple of it (price divided by earnings).
- [Add-backs when you sell a business: what buyers accept](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/add-backs-what-buyers-accept): Buyers tend to accept add-backs that are documented and clearly personal or clearly one-off, and to reject ones that are vague, recurring or needed to run the business. An add-back is an expense in your books, such as your own salary or a one-off legal bill, that a new owner would not have to pay.
- [What is my business worth? How to value a business for sale](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/what-is-my-small-business-worth): Most small businesses are valued as a multiple of what they earn for their owner. In the International Business Brokers Association's Q2 2026 survey of brokers, the multiple for sales under $2 million ran from 2.0 to 3.1 times seller's discretionary earnings (the owner's pay and profit combined). Where yours lands depends on factors such as whether a buyer can verify the earnings and whether it works without you.
- [What is a quality of earnings report, and do you need one to sell?](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/what-is-a-quality-of-earnings-report): A quality of earnings report (QoE) is an independent accountant's check of whether a business's profit is real, repeats and would carry over to a new owner. It is not an audit. You don't have to order one. But since October 1, 2026, a lender making an SBA 7(a) loan to a new owner must obtain one if the business price, not counting real estate, is $3 million or more.
- [How to make your business run without you](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/make-your-business-run-without-you): To make a business less dependent on its owner, move three things to your team: customer relationships, day-to-day decisions, and the knowledge of how things are done. Start by taking a two-week break and writing down everything that waited for you. Plan on about a year to make a visible difference; a business with a capable manager already in place may need less.
- [Customer concentration: how much is too much when you sell?](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/customer-concentration-how-much-is-too-much): There is no official limit. One business broker writing on Divestopedia says buyers are typically concerned once a single customer passes 10% of revenue; another broker treats 30% as real cash flow risk. A big customer doesn't have to stop a sale, but it can lower the price or change the terms. Contracts, a long track record and relationships beyond you can reduce the worry.
- [Documents needed to sell a business: the due diligence list](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/documents-buyers-and-lenders-ask-for): Buyers and lenders ask for three years of financial statements and tax returns, current-year figures, sales by customer, the lease, key contracts, licenses, an equipment list and employee details. A lender on an SBA-backed purchase also checks your tax returns against IRS records itself. Having it all in one organized folder before you list tends to make due diligence faster and smoother.
- [Letter of intent to purchase a business: what's in it and what to negotiate](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/letter-of-intent-to-purchase-a-business): A letter of intent (LOI) is a buyer's written offer. It sets the price, how it is paid and the main terms before lawyers draft the contract. Price and structure usually do not bind, but confidentiality and exclusivity usually do, so signing means you stop talking to other buyers for an agreed period. Settle your cash at close, exclusivity and role afterwards before you sign.
- [Asset sale vs stock sale: what's the difference when you sell a small business?](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/asset-sale-vs-stock-sale): In an asset sale, the buyer purchases what the business owns, such as equipment, inventory, customer relationships and goodwill, and you keep the company itself. In a stock sale, the buyer purchases the company, with its history and its obligations. An LLC has no stock, so the stock-style version is a sale of membership interests.
- [Seller financing when you sell a business: how a seller note works](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/seller-financing-when-selling-a-business): Seller financing means you accept part of the price after closing. The buyer signs a promissory note, called a seller note, and repays you with interest over time. In Q2 2026 data from the IBBA (International Business Brokers Association), seller financing was 6% to 11% of the price. With a Small Business Administration (SBA) loan, a note counted toward the required equity must get no payments while that loan lasts.
- [What is an earn-out when you sell your business?](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/what-is-an-earn-out): An earn-out is part of your sale price that the buyer pays after closing, and only if the business hits targets you both agreed, usually for revenue or profit. IBBA's Q2 2026 data put it at about 1% of deal value under $5 million. It is not allowed when the buyer uses an SBA 7(a) loan. If one is offered, ask how much of the result you still control.
- [Selling to a buyer with an SBA loan: what changes for you](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/selling-to-a-buyer-with-an-sba-loan): When your buyer uses an SBA 7(a) loan, the lender's rules change several things for you. In the usual case, a lender-ordered valuation must support the price, your financials are checked against tax transcripts, earn-outs are banned, and you can stay on only as a consultant for up to 24 months. A seller note on full standby can cover up to half of the buyer's required equity.
- [How to sell an HVAC, plumbing or electrical business](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/selling-an-hvac-plumbing-or-electrical-business): To sell an HVAC, plumbing or electrical business, show buyers what they pay for: recurring service-agreement revenue, licensed technicians who will stay, a business that doesn't depend on your license or relationships, and books a lender can verify. In HVAC, private-equity-backed groups are active buyers. A buyer with an SBA loan limits your role after the sale.

## Questions and answers
### How do I get my business ready to sell?
Buyers and their lenders look at five things: financial records they can verify, a business that can run without its owner, a customer base that is not concentrated in one or two accounts, operations and paperwork that transfer cleanly, and a price with evidence behind it. Getting ready means fixing the gaps in each before a buyer sees the business. Our free ten-minute readiness score shows you where you stand on all five.

### When should I start preparing?
Ideally six to twelve months before you list, because some fixes, such as moving customer relationships to your team, take time. It is still worth doing if you are about to list, or if your business has been listed for a while without selling.

### What does Handover cost?
The readiness score and a 45-minute review call are free. The Sale-Ready Package is a fixed fee: from $5,000 for a business worth under $1 million, from $10,000 for $1 million to $3 million, and from $15,000 for $3 million to $10 million. Half is due when we start and half when we hand back. We never take a percentage of your sale.

### What do I get for that?
Three years of financials recast to show true owner earnings, a customer and revenue analysis, the written story of your business for buyers, an organized document room, a fix-it list ranked by value, and an indicative value range for today and with the gaps closed.

### How long does it take?
Four weeks from kick-off to hand-back, and about five hours of your time: gathering documents, one ninety-minute conversation, and checking the facts in what we write.

### Are you business brokers?
No. We do not list businesses, find or speak to buyers, negotiate, or take success fees. We prepare the business and its documents, and you then sell it through the broker of your choice, or on your own. We also do not give formal valuations, or tax or legal advice.

### What are recast financials?
Small-business accounts are prepared for tax reporting, not to show a buyer the cash flow available to an owner. Recasting presents the same records in the way buyers and lenders assess them. It restates three years of results to show true owner earnings (often called seller’s discretionary earnings, or SDE), by adding back the owner’s above-market pay, personal expenses run through the business and one-off costs. Each adjustment is tied to a document, so a buyer’s accountant and a bank can rely on it.

### Will anyone find out I am thinking of selling?
No. We deal only with you. We never contact your staff, customers, suppliers or competitors, and nothing you share leaves us without your say-so.

### What size of business do you work with?
Owner-run businesses worth up to about $10 million, in any industry. We work with owners at different stages, from those planning several years ahead to those already preparing to list.
